title: No worst
hookLine: Hopkins's darkest sonnets say the despair out loud, and find a comfort that serves in a whirlwind
tomorrow: on a couch, eyes shut, what does a poet suddenly see?

cards: Some playlists are only sad songs, and people defend them fiercely: sometimes you need music that doesn't try to cheer you up. In a dark stretch of his life, Hopkins wrote a few sonnets like that.
Some readers call them the terrible sonnets. He told his friend Robert Bridges that one of them was written in blood. It opens: "No worst, there is none."
So what does faith say when no comfort is left? First, it says exactly that.

teach.b: The poem doesn't pretend. "Comforter, where, where is your comforting? / Mary, mother of us, where is your relief?" He calls on the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, and on Mary, and asks where they've gone.
Then: "O the mind, mind has mountains; cliffs of fall / Frightful, sheer, no-man-fathomed." The only shelter he finds is small: "a comfort serves in a whirlwind", just enough to creep under.
Here's the Christian answer the poem stands on: lament is itself prayer. You can tell God that God seems absent, and still be talking to God.
On the cross, Jesus cries out with a psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"

And that whirlwind points somewhere older, to a neighbor's scripture. In the Hebrew Bible, Job loses everything and says: "Let the day perish wherein I was born". His friends defend God and explain his suffering.
Then "the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind", and at the end, God says the friends were the ones who spoke wrongly.

Jewish tradition kept Job's complaint in its scripture, and keeps lament in its calendar: on Tisha B'Av, the book of Lamentations is read aloud. That's what the two share: the dark is allowed to speak to God.

The difference is in the voices. Hopkins, a Catholic priest, cries to the Comforter and to Mary, mother of us, under the shadow of the cross. In Job's book, God answers him directly, out of the storm.

how: Many Christians pray the psalms of lament, some especially in Holy Week, and Jews read Lamentations aloud on Tisha B'Av.

o: the opening of Hopkins's sonnet of utter despair
a promise that nothing worse can happen now
a priest's motto for staying hopeful in pain

games.q: the dark and the storm: tap the pairs.
p: a Christian name for the Holy Spirit
cursed the day he was born, argued with God
the day Lamentations is read aloud

s: Hopkins's dark sonnets hide his despair behind pretty words
they say it straight: no worst, there is none.
in the Book of Job, God answers out of a whirlwind
the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind.
Job's friends are praised in the end for explaining his suffering
at the end, God says the friends were the ones who spoke wrongly.

games.q: at a funeral, a friend says she's furious at God and feels guilty for it. what fits what Hopkins and Job share?
o: both speak their anguish to God; saying it is still a way of turning toward God.
both teach that a faithful person keeps feelings like that silent.
both teach that anger at God ends faith, so she should step away.
games.why: Hopkins asks the Comforter where the comforting is; Job curses his birthday and argues with God. both traditions keep these words as faith, not as its failure.

practice: For two minutes, bring to mind someone in a dark season, and that someone may be you. Don't fix it or look for the bright side; just say, inside, that it's hard and that it counts.
Hopkins and Job said it to God, honestly; that way is open too.

wordCard.voice: No worst: the opening of one of Hopkins's dark sonnets. It says the grief has no floor, and still, line by line, it keeps addressing God.

orig.note: Hebrew: storm, whirlwind. In Job 38:1 the LORD answers Job out of the storm, the whirlwind behind Hopkins's line.

carryVoice: Carry this: comfort serves in a whirlwind, small, but enough to creep under. Rest well.
